summary: A profile of Todd Harrison, a 57-year-old veteran lineworker in Morgan County, who reflects on how renewable energy, storage, smart grids and predictive tools have changed the fight against power outages. He traces the shift from a coal-and-gas, routine-driven era to one of distributed generation, real-time data and microgrids. He concludes outages are now less frequent and severe, with lineworkers acting as troubleshooters and system optimizers.
one_line: Veteran lineworker Todd Harrison recounts how renewables, storage, smart grids and forecasting have reshaped the fight against power outages over two decades.
key_facts: Todd Harrison is a 57-year-old veteran lineworker in Morgan County, interviewed on October 12, 2023 after scaling a tower.
In the early 2000s, power was mostly coal and gas; renewables were not main players and fighting outages was 'almost like a guessing game intertwined with relentless routine.'
By September 10, 2025, households generating power with rooftop panels and turbines were becoming part of Todd's daily work.
Todd says integrating intermittent sources means keeping the grid stable 'when the sun ducks behind clouds or the wind dies down.'
On September 26, 2026, a powerful storm hit the state; homes with solar-battery systems stayed lit and communities with small wind farms recovered sooner, which Todd calls 'a turning point.'
By the late 2020s, battery technologies had improved sharply in cost and efficiency, making storing renewable energy economical and reducing pressure on lineworkers.
In October 2027, Todd observed control rooms becoming more sophisticated, with real-time data flowing in, requiring lineworkers to work with information as well as their hands.
By September 2030, enhanced weather forecasting and predictive maintenance had significantly decreased the time Todd spent in the field under emergency conditions.
By 2032, significant capital had been invested in 'smart grid' infrastructure that can reroute power and isolate outages, replacing the manual rerouting of Todd's early days.
By the mid-2030s, public sentiment and policy were driving toward a decarbonized future with more renewables on the grid.
In the present, distributed generation and robust storage make outages less frequent and less severe, and lineworkers are now troubleshooters and system optimizers.
